## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes linked to land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation, however, but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their cumulative impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@oliver2014interactions; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number]. Given these complexities, forecasting changes to biodiversity exposed to multiple global change drivers will require an understanding of the mechanisms underlying the multifactorial nature of global change drivers.

One of the major mechanisms through which many of these drivers may affect plant community composition and diversity is through changes in community biomass, which in turn change the magnitude for competition for resources [@grime1973competitive; @chesson2000mechanisms]. Warming and nitrogen addition typically increase community biomass (@fig-concept a) [@proulx1998reversal; @post2008opposing; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @zhou2020responses; @collins2022global; @Speiser2022-st; @borer2024planning], which can thus shift the intensity and nature of the dominant plant-plant interactions. Specifically, this may lead to communities with taller, faster growing species which are stronger competitors, especially for light [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. Grazing removes community biomass [@frank2005interactive; @Bernes2015-yg], while also nutrients from urine and dung, and so impacts on community biomass are variable but can lead to increased diversity [@Austrheim2001-nu; @frank2005interactive; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @song2020grazing]. We therefore propose that we could simplify and synthesize across multiple global change drivers by using community biomass as a *common currency*, which reflects the magnitude of their impacts on competitive interactions. If so, we predict that incorporating community biomass in models of community response to global change drivers account for the direct and interacting impact of those drivers (@fig-concept b).

![Two alternative hypotheses for how three global change drivers warming, nitrogen addition and clipping (or grazing) affect plant diversity. a) Warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping (or grazing) affect diversity directly, or b) these drivers affect diversity indirectly, mediated through community biomass as a *common currency*.](figures/Figure1_hypotheses.png){#fig-concept width="600"}

We test this prediction with a global change experiment in mountain grasslands, because they harbor unique biodiversity and provide important ecosystem functions and services such as carbon sequestration, water cycling, and grazing pastures; underpinning the lives and livelihoods of hundreds of millions of people [@egan2017mountain]. We manipulate three common global change drivers in a field experiment: climate warming (transplant to lower elevation), nitrogen deposition (fertilizing using seven levels ranging between 0 and 100 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^), and clipping at two different intensities or natural grazing (@fig-methods).

Plant community responses to global change drivers often differ along environmental gradients and across habitats [@milchunas1993quantitative; @elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @delnevo2018plastic; @Vandvik2020-hu]. To assess the degree of context-dependency and how community responses are mediated through community biomass, we repeated the experiment in two different environments, an alpine and a sub-alpine grassland community in Western Norway. Montane grasslands in Norway are transhumance-based grazing systems [@reinton1955seter; @austad2004overview], grazed by domestic and natural grazers with the extant grazing pressure decreasing with elevation [@halbritter2025effects; @halbritter2025data]. The two sites represent different annual and growing season temperatures, with the alpine site being more temperature and nutrient limited (Supplementary Figures S1). By replicating the experiment in two different environmental contexts we can test the generality of our hypothesis [@fraser2013coordinated].

We hypothesize that these global change drivers affect diversity and species composition mediated through community biomass, resulting in more competitive interactions, but alternative mechanisms are possible. For example, some species may be physiologically intolerant of very high or low temperature and therefore go locally extinct or successfully colonize, regardless of the competitive environment (REFs). Second, increased nitrogen addition, especially at high levels, can lead to acidic soil conditions [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity due to differences in tolerance to acidic conditions, independently of competitive interactions. Similarly, some species may be particularly tolerant or intolerant to direct effects of grazing irrespective of competitive interactions [@archibald2019unified]. Such shifts in species composition might therefore not be mediated through community biomass. Ecological indicator values can be used to describe species community composition in response to environmental affinities and can provide further insights into the mechanisms of these dynamics [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range].

Here we used a field experiment in montane grasslands in Western Norway, replicated across two sites, to test if global change drivers operate through the same mechanism on diversity and understanding alternative mechanisms. We used a split-plot design, exposing plant communities to three single global change drivers and their interactions, namely warmer climate, atmospheric nitrogen addition, and clipping or grazing (@fig-methods). Different nitrogen levels were applied at the block level and each plot within a block received a combination of warming and clipping or grazing treatments. Plant communities moved to lower elevation experienced an approximately 3°C increase in average growing season temperature (air: 3.09 ± 0.186 °C, ground: 3.06 ± 0.176 °C, and soil: 2.82 ± 0.142 °C; Supplementary Figure S1, Table S1). We applied a large range of nitrogen levels to simulate nitrogen addition close to and well beyond the current atmospheric nitrogen deposition in the mountains in south-western Norway [@aas2023monitoring] (2-3 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^) and the critical load for change in species composition in alpine grasslands [@bobbink2011review] (c. 5-10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^). Our understanding of environmentally extreme conditions is limited, and such simulations can provide a mechanistic understanding of thresholds for community change [@Kayler2015-pr]. We simulated grazing by clipping because our main interest was in the effect of biomass removal, however, we also had naturally grazed plots outside the fenced area to account for the difference between grazing by animals and clipping. After three years of global change treatments, we harvested community biomass at peak growing season and assessed the change in vascular plant species composition and diversity.
